Q845.L1t: Clothing is one of the most visible ways people express their values and lifestyles.
Q845.L2t: The passage notes that a researcher in Michigan studied attitudes toward dress as early as 1955.
Q845.L3t: The passage says that dress has become more varied and colorful, that white and blue collar workers both came to see dress as a basis for being judged, and that its importance has not lessened but has been confirmed by recent research across many groups.
Q845.L4t: The passage mainly suggests that people have come to recognize dress as increasingly important.
Q845.L2f: The Michigan researcher's study was carried out in the 1990s and looked only at teenagers' fashion choices.
Q845.L3f: The passage says that concern for clothes remains an exclusively female matter, and that research shows women are the only group who care about how dress shapes impressions.
Q845.L4f: The passage mainly suggests that women always love beautiful dresses.

Q760.L1t: Butterflies are among the best-known insects in Britain, and many people enjoy seeing them in gardens and the countryside.
Q760.L2t: The Big Butterfly Count is a yearly survey run by the charity Butterfly Conservation, which Sir David Attenborough leads as President.
Q760.L3t: Attenborough describes the count as a way for people to contribute to discovering the butterflies and other wildlife that share their gardens, parks and countryside, and the passage calls it a yearly survey of butterflies across the nation.
Q760.L4t: The annual Big Butterfly Count is meant to survey and study the butterflies found across Britain.
Q760.L2f: The Big Butterfly Count is a competition held every four years to find the most beautiful butterfly in British gardens.
Q760.L3f: The passage describes the Big Butterfly Count as a campaign run by the charity to train the public in gardening methods that help butterflies and other wildlife thrive.
Q760.L4f: The annual Big Butterfly Count is meant to teach people how to garden well.

Q803.L1t: Nelson Mandela was a South African leader who spent 27 years in prison and was famous worldwide.
Q803.L2t: Mandela enjoyed boxing and long-distance running in his youth and kept up daily exercise even while in prison.
Q803.L3t: In his autobiography Mandela says he did not enjoy the violence of boxing so much as the science of it, and he was curious about how one moves, plans attack and retreat, and paces oneself over a match.
Q803.L4t: Mandela loved boxing because he appreciated its strategy and the skill involved.
Q803.L2f: Mandela took up boxing only after his release from prison in 1990 and trained at a professional gym in Cape Town.
Q803.L3f: In his autobiography Mandela says that what drew him to boxing most was the thrill of the violence and the fight itself, not its technique.
Q803.L4f: Mandela loved boxing because he enjoyed its violence.
